fixes.explanation: Judah it is, friend. The LORD answers, “Judah shall go up…” and that's one name with no confusion. Most group chats need forty messages just to decide who's driving.
Dan is a fair pick, but it isn't the tribe the LORD names. When the Israelites ask who goes up first, He answers, “Judah shall go up…” Judah is the name in His answer, friend.

Guarding isn't part of Judah's offer, friend. They ask the Simeonites, “Come up with us to our allotted territory, and let us fight against the Canaanites.” Then comes the return: “And we likewise will go with you to your territory.” It's fighting side by side, and that's the swap.
Not this time, baker. The verse ends, “So the Simeonites went with them.” That means they took Judah's offer. Judah asks and Simeon goes, just like brothers.

Judah doesn't turn away from Jerusalem, friend. Verse 8 says the men of Judah “fought against Jerusalem and captured it.” The same verse says they put the city to the sword and set it on fire. I think that's a heavy verse to read.

That's the offer, friend. Caleb, one of Moses' spies (Numbers 13:6), says, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.” He's offering a marriage to the man who captures the city. That's a long way from the free cookie I hand out.

Silver doesn't come up in Caleb's offer, friend. He says, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.” What he offers is a marriage to Acsah, not a share of the city's silver.

There's no seat among the elders in this offer, friend. Caleb says, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.” The offer is a marriage to Acsah, with no title or chair attached.

Gideon son of Joash shows up later in Judges (Judges 6:29), but he isn't in this story. Here, the text names Othniel, son of Caleb's younger brother Kenaz, as the man who captured the city. Gideon's chapters are still ahead, friend.

Springs of water, baker. Acsah says, “Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well.” I think she knows land is better with water. That's like me having a bakery with a lovely counter and no oven. Caleb gives her both the upper and lower springs.
Right, friend. The text says the descendants of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenite, went up with the men of Judah. Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the link. They went to live among the people.

Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5), isn't who the text names. These are the descendants of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenite. Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the family connection. They go up with the men of Judah and live among the people.

Esau, Jacob's twin brother (Genesis 25:25-26), isn't in this verse. The group that goes up with Judah is the descendants of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenite. Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the link. They head to the Wilderness of Judah and settle among the people.

Hormah is right. After Judah and the Simeonites attack Zephath and devote the city to destruction, the text says, “So it was called Hormah.” The city goes from Zephath to Hormah in a single verse. My sign out front takes a whole weekend and a ladder.

Chariots of iron, friend. The verse says the LORD was with Judah, and they took possession of the hill country, “but they could not drive out the inhabitants of the plains because they had chariots of iron.” That's the reason the text gives, and it gives no other.

Othniel is the one who captured Kiriath-sepher, and Caleb gave him Acsah in marriage (Judges 1:13). Hebron is a different place, though. The verse says, “Just as Moses had promised, Judah gave Hebron to Caleb…” Othniel's name isn't in that verse.
Phinehas is Aaron's grandson (Exodus 6:25), but he isn't in this passage. The text says, “Just as Moses had promised, Judah gave Hebron to Caleb…” Caleb is the name to remember here, friend.
